That, Viktoriya Sergeyevna, was a wish lost due to a ridiculous mistake.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'head chef' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The head chef manages the entire kitchen.

examples.text: Они привели нового шеф-повара прямо из Индии.
examples.trans: They brought a new chef straight from India.

examples.text: Шеф-повар решит, подходите ли вы ресторану.
examples.trans: The head chef will decide whether you suit the restaurant.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'from', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: A letter from Mum.
I'm tired of work.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'God' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Thank God!
No, thank God.

examples.text: О, наконец тепло! Слава богу. Сейчас ещё чай сделаю.
examples.trans: Oh, it's warm at last! Thank goodness. Now I'll make some tea too.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лавиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'glory be to / hail'.

related.gloss: not to glory be to (negated infinitive)

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и славиться вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and glory be to on time.

examples.text: На нашей кухне все умеют славиться.
examples.trans: In our kitchen everyone knows how to glory be to.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'ages' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The monastery is eight centuries old.
That was in the last century.

examples.text: Наш с вами город очень старый. Почти четыре века здесь были набеги.
examples.trans: Our town is very old. For almost four centuries there were raids here.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'no', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: No, it's mine.
No? All right.
No. That's mine.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'Mishanya' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть мишаня.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always Mishanya.
The chef immediately noticed where the Mishanya was.

meanings.note: Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'singing' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть пение.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always singing.
The chef immediately noticed where the singing was.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, it (is)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's mine.
And this is for you.
And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.
Chef, I didn't take it.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'your', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: This is your coffee.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.
Your boss is here.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'now', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Now I'm the boss.
Now everything's fine.

examples.text: Теперь я начальник нашей стройки. Ты уволен!
examples.trans: Now I'm the boss of our building site. You're fired!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'will'.

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to crow like a rooster'.

related.gloss: to to crow like a rooster (prefixed perfective)
not to to crow like a rooster (negated infinitive)

examples.trans: Who will crow?

examples.text: И кто тогда будет громко кукарекать?
examples.trans: And who will loudly crow then?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'come on, well', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh, come on, Dad!
Well?

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'without', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's no problem.
This time there's no trick.
That's no problem at all.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'pants' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The pants are too long.
Are the pants too long for Slavik?

examples.text: Ты почему стоишь передо мной без штанов?
examples.trans: Why are you standing in front of me without pants?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what, that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'играть').

examples.trans: I lost it on the stock exchange.
Our team lost.

examples.text: Денег нет, Самсон. Я их на бирже проиграл.
examples.trans: There is no money, Samson. I lost it on the stock exchange.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'because of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Из-за вашей Лёли весь класс зовёт меня врунишкой!
examples.trans: Because of your Lyolya the whole class calls me a little liar!
We were late because of the rain.

examples.text: А трава в мешках сгорела. Из-за вас!
examples.trans: And the herbs in the sacks burned. Because of you!

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'лепый'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('ridiculous / absurd').

examples.trans: Ridiculous words.

examples.text: Я сейчас лично проверю эти нелепые слова!
examples.trans: I will personally check these ridiculous words right now!

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'mistake' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is some kind of mistake!
Sorry, I made a mistake.
There are many serious mistakes in the case.

meanings.note: Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'wish' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть желание.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always wish.
The chef immediately noticed where the wish was.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ейчас').

examples.trans: I'm in the office now.
I'll be right there.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'rematch' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть реванш.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always rematch.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'about', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm thinking about it.

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'кладываться'). meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'go, walk', paired with 'пойти'.

examples.trans: I'm going home.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и тренироваться вовремя.
